---
title: "Interest Rates"
---

```{R}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
library(fbi)
```

FRED-MD (McCracken and Ng, `research.stlouisfed.org/econ/mccracken/fred-databases`) is a monthly panel of ~127 US macroeconomic and financial series, each with a recommended stationarity transform (log, difference, log-difference). We look at three short-term interest rates, each first-differenced:

- `FEDFUNDS`: effective federal funds rate, set by FOMC policy
- `TB3MS`: 3-month Treasury bill rate
- `TB6MS`: 6-month Treasury bill rate

Treasury bill rates track the federal funds rate closely under normal conditions, since short-term Treasury yields price in the expected path of Fed policy. The mean-shift mechanism here is real and dated: the Fed held the funds rate near zero from December 2008 to December 2015 (post-financial-crisis ZIRP) and again from March 2020 to March 2022 (COVID), with a rapid hiking cycle in between and after. We restrict to 2000-2022, which brackets both zero-rate episodes plus the 2015-2018 and 2022-2023 hiking cycles.

```{R}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| label: interest-rates-load

filepath <- "../data/real-data/FRED-2026-05.csv"
fred_data <- fredmd(filepath, date_start = NULL, date_end = NULL, transform = TRUE) |>
  rm_outliers.fredmd()

X_data <- as_tibble(fred_data) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2000-01-01"), date <= as.Date("2022-12-01")) |>
  dplyr::select(date, FEDFUNDS, TB3MS, TB6MS) |>
  drop_na()

X_mat <- as.matrix(X_data[, c("FEDFUNDS", "TB3MS", "TB6MS")])
win   <- 12
```

Lag-1 autocorrelation on the raw differenced series is around 0.7, so we compare against a 12-month rolling-mean baseline (`rolling_mean()`), the same pattern used for Air Pollution's slow seasonal drift, rather than a hard PELT segmentation.

```{R}
#| echo: false
#| label: interest-rates-residuals

X_roll  <- apply(X_mat, 2, rolling_mean, window = win)
colnames(X_roll) <- colnames(X_mat)
X_resid <- X_mat - X_roll
```

```{R}
#| echo: false
#| label: interest-rates-tables

cor_tables <- function(X_mat, X_resid) {
  ece_cor <- ece.cor(X_mat) |> round(3)
  rownames(ece_cor) <- colnames(ece_cor) <- colnames(X_mat)

  X_resid_complete <- X_resid[complete.cases(X_resid), ]
  rolling_cor <- cor(X_resid_complete) |> round(3)
  pearson_cor <- cor(X_mat) |> round(3)

  ece_pmat     <- ece_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)
  rolling_pmat <- cor_pval(X_resid_complete) |> round(3)
  pearson_pmat <- cor_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)

  list(ece_cor = ece_cor, rolling_cor = rolling_cor, pearson_cor = pearson_cor,
       ece_pmat = ece_pmat, rolling_pmat = rolling_pmat, pearson_pmat = pearson_pmat)
}

tab_full <- cor_tables(X_mat, X_resid)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Plot

```{R fig-interest-rates-series}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Monthly change in FEDFUNDS, TB3MS, TB6MS, 2000-2022. Blue = 12-month rolling mean."
#| fig-height: 7

X_long <- X_data |>
  bind_cols(as.data.frame(X_roll) |> rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_roll"), everything())) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -date, names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(
    type = if_else(str_ends(series, "_roll"), "Rolling Mean", "Raw"),
    rate = str_remove(series, "_roll$")
  )

ggplot(X_long, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
  geom_line(data = ~ filter(.x, type == "Raw"), color = "gray50", alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = ~ filter(.x, type == "Rolling Mean"), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  facet_wrap(~rate, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Monthly Change in Short-Term Rates", x = NULL, y = "Percentage points",
       caption = "Source: FRED-MD") +
  theme_minimal()
```

All three series spend long stretches pinned near zero during ZIRP, then swing sharply during the 2004-2006, 2015-2018, and 2022-2023 hiking cycles. The rolling mean tracks these regimes but lags at the turning points.

## Correlation

```{R}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(tab_full$ece_cor,     caption = "ECE Correlation")
knitr::kable(tab_full$rolling_cor, caption = "Rolling Correlation")
knitr::kable(tab_full$pearson_cor, caption = "Pearson Correlation")
```

Pearson says all three rates move together: 0.79-0.95. A 12-month rolling mean pulls FEDFUNDS-TB3MS and FEDFUNDS-TB6MS down to around 0.62-0.64, but TB3MS-TB6MS barely moves (0.92). ECE tells a different story: TB3MS-TB6MS stays high (0.85), but FEDFUNDS drops to essentially **zero** with both bill rates (-0.20, -0.20). Once the ZIRP-driven mean shifts are accounted for, month-to-month changes in the funds rate carry no leftover information about month-to-month changes in bill rates, even though bill rates still move tightly with each other.

## P-Values

```{R}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(tab_full$ece_pmat,     caption = "ECE P-Values")
knitr::kable(tab_full$rolling_pmat, caption = "Rolling P-Values")
knitr::kable(tab_full$pearson_pmat, caption = "Pearson P-Values")
```

Pearson and Rolling both reject independence for every pair (p < 0.001). ECE rejects TB3MS-TB6MS (p < 0.001) but not FEDFUNDS-TB3MS (p = 0.24) or FEDFUNDS-TB6MS (p = 0.27). The naive correlation between FEDFUNDS and the bill rates looks like a real relationship, but it is largely the two ZIRP episodes lining up in all three series at once, not genuine co-movement in the funds rate's monthly changes.

:::

## Bootstrap Methods

```{R}
#| echo: false
ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.multiplier")
ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.parametric")
```

## Where this leaves us

FRED-MD as a whole is a hard testbed for ECE. Most of its 127 series are already first- or second-differenced, and differencing tends to push segment-level variance toward zero, which makes ECE's correlation estimates volatile (see the appendix vignette, `vignettes/FRED.qmd`, for examples across housing starts, exchange rates, and industrial production). This triplet is an exception: FEDFUNDS, TB3MS, and TB6MS give a clean, stable divergence between Pearson and ECE, driven by a real and dated mechanism (Fed policy regime changes) rather than an estimation artifact. The result is also economically sensible: a change in the funds rate itself doesn't predict the *change* in bill rates once you've separated genuine month-to-month co-movement from both series sharing the same zero-rate and hiking episodes. Whether this holds up as a general pattern in short-term interest rates, or is specific to this window and this triplet, is worth checking against other maturities and other tightening cycles.
